title: Elmvale's Minty family wins court case against police
subtitle: Supreme Court rules on police consulting lawyer before completing notes.
article: Elmvale's Minty family has been awarded court costs following a Supreme court decision released today.
The family argued it's not fair for police officers to speak with a lawyer before documenting what took place in a serious situation.
The Minty family launched the legal battle after Douglas Minty, 59, a developmentally delayed man who lived with his mom, Evelyn, was shot and killed by a Huronia West OPP officer in 2009.
Minty was walking down the driveway toward Const. Graham Seguin with a pocket knife in his hand.
After being told to drop the weapon, Minty continued towards Seguin and was shot five times.
A senior officer arrived at the scene and told all of the officers there not to make notes until they had consulted with a lawyer.
The lawsuit was co-filed by the Schaeffer family.
Levi Schaeffer, 32, a man with mental illness, was also shot and killed by an OPP officer in the summer of 2009.
A Toronto Star investigation revealed police notes were written two days after Schaeffer was killed and after officers consulted with the same lawyer.
Both families questioned the legality of the practice.
Police argued they have the right to talk to a lawyer before finalizing their notes.

"Consulting with counsel at the note-making stage impinges on the ability of police officers to prepare accurate, detailed and comprehensive notes in accordance with their duty," Justice Michael Moldaver wrote on behalf of the panel.

"It creates an 'appearances problem'... A reasonable member of the public would naturally question whether counsel's assistance at the note-making stage is sought by officers to help them fulfill their duties, or if it is instead sought, in their self-interest, to protect themselves and their colleagues from the potential liability of an adverse Special Investigations Unit investigation."
In talking with a lawyer, the panel said the tone of the notes shifts from explaining what happened "toward a more sophisticated explanation for why the incident occurred."

As an example, the panel said notes made by Acting Sgt. Mark Pullbrook - an officer involved in the Schaeffer case - were completely different the day of the shooting when compared to the way he routinely took notes.
The ruling said an officer getting even basic legal advice for prepping notes is "meaningless" and notes should be an independent account of the events, in officers' own words.
Once notes are made, then an officer can seek legal counsel, the ruling said.
